name: Striped Bass
diet: Menhaden and other small fish, crabs
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Silver body with 7 to 8 dark stripes running from head to tail
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Summer Flounder (Fluke)
idTips: Flat body with both eyes on the left side; brown with eye-like spots
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

climate.note: As the Atlantic warms, the center of the summer flounder population has moved north along the East Coast, so more are now found off New England.

name: Bluefish
idTips: Blue-green back, silver sides, and a large jaw with sharp teeth
whatToDo: Handle carefully because of the sharp teeth.

name: Atlantic Sturgeon
bestTime: Any time; feeds along the bottom
idTips: Long body with rows of bony plates, a shark-like tail, and whisker-like barbels
whatToDo: Release immediately with as little handling as possible. It is illegal to keep.

name: Red Lionfish
idTips: Red and white stripes with long, fan-like spines
whatToDo: The spines are venomous, so do not touch. Removal is encouraged; report sightings to your state wildlife agency.

climate.note: Lionfish cannot survive cold winter water. As winters warm, they may be able to live farther north along the Atlantic coast.

name: Atlantic Cod
bestTime: Day and night near the bottom
habitat: Rocky and gravel bottoms in cold water
idTips: Three dorsal fins, a chin barbel, and a pale line along the side
whatToDo: The population in New England is low. Check current rules before fishing.

climate.note: The Gulf of Maine is one of the fastest-warming ocean areas. Warmer water is linked to poorer survival of young cod, which makes recovery of the population harder.

parasite.note: Often carries "codworm" (a roundworm larva) in its flesh. Seals are the worm's final host, so codworm is more common where seal numbers have recovered.
parasite.foodSafety: Cook to 145°F, or freeze before eating raw or lightly cured.
parasite.source: NOAA Fisheries; FDA Fish and Fishery Products Hazards and Controls Guidance

name: European Green Crab
habitat: Tide pools, salt marshes, and mudflats
idTips: Five spines on each side of the shell behind the eyes; color varies and is not always green
whatToDo: Never move it or release it somewhere else. Report sightings where it is new.

climate.note: Milder winters let more green crabs survive, which has helped their numbers grow in New England and spread along the Pacific coast.

name: North Atlantic Right Whale
diet: Tiny copepods filtered from the water
habitat: Cape Cod Bay and coastal waters
idTips: Dark body with no dorsal fin, rough white patches on the head, and a V-shaped blow
whatToDo: Federal law requires staying at least 500 yards away.

climate.note: Warming in the Gulf of Maine has moved the tiny copepods these whales eat, so the whales now spend more time in new areas such as Cape Cod Bay and the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

name: Common Snook
idTips: Sleek silver body with a bold black line along the side and a sloped forehead
whatToDo: Sensitive to cold. Follow Florida seasons and slot limits.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

climate.note: Snook die in cold snaps. With fewer hard freezes, their range has been spreading farther north along Florida's coasts.
climate.source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Tarpon
idTips: Large silver scales, an upturned mouth, and a long last ray on the dorsal fin
whatToDo: Mostly caught and released. Keep large fish in the water when possible.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Smalltooth Sawfish
bestTime: Any time; often in shallow water
idTips: Flat, shark-like body with a long, flat snout lined with teeth on both sides
whatToDo: Never keep one. Leave it in the water, cut the line as close to the hook as is safe, and report the encounter.

name: Red Drum (Redfish)
bestTime: Morning and evening on moving tides
idTips: Copper-bronze body with one or more black spots near the tail
whatToDo: Follow local slot limits.

parasite.note: Larger fish often have "spaghetti worms" (tapeworm larvae) in the flesh. They do not infect people.
parasite.foodSafety: Safe to eat when cooked. Cut out any worms you see.

name: Spotted Seatrout
idTips: Silvery-gray with scattered black spots on the back and tail; two large front teeth
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

parasite.note: Anglers often find "spaghetti worms" (tapeworm larvae) in the flesh, especially in warmer months. They do not infect people.
parasite.foodSafety: Safe to eat when cooked. Cut out any worms you see.

name: Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtle
habitat: Shallow Gulf waters, bays, and nesting beaches
idTips: The smallest sea turtle, with a round gray-olive shell
whatToDo: Do not approach or touch. Report nesting or stranded turtles to local authorities.

climate.note: Sand temperature decides whether a turtle egg hatches as male or female. Warmer nesting beaches produce more females.

name: California Halibut
habitat: Sandy bottoms near shore and in bays
idTips: Flat body that can have eyes on either side; a large mouth that reaches past the eye
whatToDo: Follow California size limits.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Kelp Bass (Calico Bass)
idTips: Olive-brown body with pale blotches in a calico pattern
whatToDo: Follow California size and bag limits.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Garibaldi
idTips: Bright orange all over; young fish have blue spots
whatToDo: California's state marine fish. It is illegal to take one.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Devilweed (invasive seaweed)
diet: Makes its own food through photosynthesis
idTips: Brown seaweed with small air bladders and fern-like leaves; can form thick mats
whatToDo: Do not move it between areas. Clean boats and gear before leaving.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Southern Sea Otter
diet: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, and snails
idTips: Small furry marine mammal that floats on its back and often uses rocks as tools
whatToDo: Give plenty of space. If an otter changes what it is doing because of you, you are too close.

name: Leopard Shark
bestTime: Daytime in shallow water, especially on rising tides
diet: Crabs, clams, worms, and small fish
habitat: Shallow bays, sandy flats, and near kelp
idTips: Slim gray shark with dark saddle bars and spots along the back
whatToDo: Harmless to people. Follow size limits.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Lingcod
idTips: Large head and mouth with sharp teeth; mottled brown-gray body
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits.
source: Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: Black Rockfish
diet: Small fish, krill, and crab larvae
idTips: Dark gray to black body with a pale belly and a spiny dorsal fin
whatToDo: Fish brought up from deep water can be injured by the pressure change. Use a descending device when releasing.
source: Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife

parasite.note: Like many Pacific rockfish, can carry Anisakis roundworm larvae. Whales, dolphins, and seals are the worm's final hosts.
parasite.foodSafety: Cook to 145°F, or freeze before eating raw.
parasite.source: FDA Fish and Fishery Products Hazards and Controls Guidance

name: Dungeness Crab
diet: Clams, small crabs, worms, and fish
idTips: Purple-brown shell with white-tipped claws
whatToDo: Only males of legal size may be kept. Check current seasons.
source: Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife

climate.note: During the 2014–2016 Pacific marine heatwave, a huge toxic algae bloom made crabs unsafe to eat and delayed the fishing season.

name: Hawaiian Monk Seal
bestTime: Rests on beaches by day, feeds at night
idTips: Gray-brown seal with no visible ear flaps; often rests on the sand
whatToDo: Stay at least 50 feet away, and 150 feet from a mother with a pup.

name: Green Sea Turtle (Honu)
habitat: Reefs, seagrass beds, and shallow coastal waters
idTips: Smooth oval shell and a small rounded head with a blunt beak
whatToDo: Stay at least 10 feet away. Never touch or feed.

climate.note: Sand temperature decides whether a turtle egg hatches as male or female. Warmer beaches produce more females.

name: Reef Triggerfish (Humuhumunukunukuapuaa)
diet: Small invertebrates, algae, and sea urchins
idTips: Hawaii's state fish; a black wedge-shaped band on the side and yellow lines near the mouth
whatToDo: Enjoy watching and do not touch the reef.

name: Roi (Peacock Grouper)
idTips: Dark brown body covered in small blue spots
whatToDo: Introduced to Hawaii in the 1950s. It can carry ciguatera toxin, so eating it is not recommended.

name: Barracuda
idTips: Large sliver body with sharp teeth and slim body
whatToDo: Handle carefully because of the sharp teeth.

name: Sheepshead
idTips: Distinct black and white stripes with human like teeth
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Cobia
habitat: Reefs, seagrass beds, and shallow coastal waters
idTips: Dark brown body with one dorsal fin and horizontal black and white stripes
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Peacock Flounder
habitat: Sandy bottoms near shore and in bays
idTips: Flat oval body with blue rings and able to change colors
whatToDo: Never move it or release it somewhere else. Report sightings where it is new.

name: Spot
bestTime: Any time; feeds along the bottom
idTips: One dark spot right behind the gill plate
whatToDo: Follow local bag limit

name: Yellowtail Amberjack
idTips: Bright yellow tail long body and a brassy yellow stripe running down its back
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits.

name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
idTips: Massive sized turtle with rubbery shell with seven raised ridges running lengthwise
whatToDo: Stay at least 150 ft away

name: Blue Crab
bestTime: Any time; often in shallow water
idTips: Olive green shell, paddle shaped rear legs, and bright red or blue claws
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Cownose Ray
habitat: Shallow bays, sandy flats, and near kelp
idTips: Two distinctive cow like snout and plain brown kite shaped body
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits as well as looking out for the venomous barb at the end

name: Bonefish
habitat: Shallow bays, sandy flats, and near kelp
idTips: A silvery long torpedo shaped white body with a pig shaped snout
whatToDo: Safely unhook it and release it or follow local size and bag limit

name: King Salmon
habitat: Shallow bays, sandy flats, and near kelp
idTips: Black spots of both sides of the tail and black color around the fishes gums
whatToDo: Follow Alaska laws about size and bag limit

name: Red snapper
idTips: Red oval shape body, red eyes, with big mouth and teeth
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Gag Grouper
idTips: Gray or brown colored body with black markings and a large Jaw
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits as well as the bag limit

name: King Mackerel
idTips: Long slandered body with a deep forked shaped tail
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Blacktip Shark
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Gray long body with black tip of the fins especially on the pectoral fin
whatToDo: Release immediately with as little handling as possible.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Spanish Mackerel
idTips: Silver body with yellowish spots and a streamlined shape.
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Bull Shark
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Broad blunt snout, stocky body and small eyes.
whatToDo: Release immediately with as little handling as possible.

name: Walleye Pollock
idTips: Elongated body, dark back and pale sides.
whatToDo: Follow Alaska laws about size and bag limit

name: Tripletail
idTips: Deep body, brown coloration, and three tail-like fins.
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Black Drum
idTips: Dark gray to black body, large scales, and chin barbels.
whatToDo: Keep or release according to local size and bag limits.

name: Florida Pompano
diet: Sea urchins, crabs, clams, and snails
idTips: Tall, flattened silver body with dark fins and deeply forked tail.
whatToDo: Keep or release according to local size and bag limits.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Wahoo
idTips: Long narrow body, sharp teeth, blue-green back, and distinctive vertical blue bars.
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Blackfin Tuna
idTips: Dark blue-black back, silver sides, and relatively short pectoral fins.
whatToDo: Keep or release according to local size and bag limits.

name: Tautog
idTips: Thick dark body, blunt head, large teeth.
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits as well as the bag limit

name: Scup
diet: Clams, small crabs, worms, and fish
idTips: Silver body with darker back and small mouth.
whatToDo: Follow local seasons and size limits

name: Atlantic croaker
idTips: Silver-gray body with faint dark markings and chin barbels
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Pacific Sanddab
idTips: Flat body with both eyes on one side.
whatToDo: Follow local bag limit
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: California Scorpionfish
idTips: Mottled reddish-brown body, large head, spiny fins.
whatToDo: Handle carefully because of sharp spines; follow local rules.

name: Arctic Grayling
idTips: Large sail-like dorsal fin with colorful spots.
whatToDo: Follow Alaska fishing regulations.

name: Kelp Greenling
idTips: Long body with mottled green, brown, or reddish coloration.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.
source: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

name: California Corbina
idTips: Silver-gray body and pointed dorsal fin.
whatToDo: Follow California regulations.

name: Cabezon
idTips: Large head, wide mouth, mottled body.
whatToDo: Check local regulations before keeping.

name: Weakfish
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Silver body with dark spots on back and fins.
whatToDo: Follow current local regulations.

name: Giant Trevally
idTips: Large muscular body, dark coloration, powerful tail.
whatToDo: Follow Hawaii regulations; handle carefully.

name: Pacific Halibut
idTips: Very large flat body with both eyes on one side.
whatToDo: Follow current halibut regulations.

name: Hogfish
idTips: Long snout, reddish-orange fins, elongated body.
whatToDo: Follow current regulations.

name: Bonnethead Shark
idTips: Shovel-shaped head and small body.
whatToDo: Follow shark regulations; release carefully.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Nurse Shark
idTips: Broad flat head, small eyes, barbels around mouth.
whatToDo: Avoid unnecessary handling; release carefully.

name: Greater Amberjack
idTips: Long body with amber stripe through the eye.
whatToDo: Check current size and possession limits.

name: Vermilion Snapper
idTips: Reddish body with pinkish sides and pointed snout.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.

name: Lane Snapper
idTips: Pinkish-red body with yellow stripes and dark spot.
whatToDo: Follow current regulations.

name: Mangrove Snapper
idTips: Gray body, dark lateral line, reddish fins.
whatToDo: Follow local size and bag limits.

name: Jack Crevalle
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Thick body, yellowish fins, dark spot near gill cover.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.

name: Permit
diet: Crabs, clams, worms, and small fish
habitat: Shallow bays, sandy flats, and near kelp
idTips: Tall, flattened silver body and deeply forked tail.
whatToDo: Follow current regulations.

name: Gray Triggerfish
diet: Small invertebrates, algae, and sea urchins
idTips: Deep compressed body and prominent dorsal spines.
whatToDo: Follow current regulations.

name: Southern Stingray
bestTime: Any time; feeds along the bottom
idTips: Diamond-shaped body and long whip-like tail.
whatToDo: Avoid stepping on it; release carefully.

name: Spadefish
bestTime: Any time; often in shallow water
idTips: Tall silver body with several dark vertical bands.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.

name: Lemon Shark
habitat: Bays, inlets, and the surf zone
idTips: Yellowish-brown body and broad snout.
whatToDo: Follow shark regulations; release carefully.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Atlantic Sharpnose Shark
bestTime: Any time; feeds along the bottom
idTips: Slim body, pointed snout, gray back and white underside.
whatToDo: Follow current shark regulations.
source: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

name: Ladyfish
bestTime: Any time; often in shallow water
idTips: Long slender silver body and deeply forked tail.
whatToDo: Often released; follow local regulations.

name: Almaco Jack
idTips: Deep-bodied jack with dark stripe through the eye.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.

name: Southern Kingfish
idTips: Slender silver body with darker back and chin barbels.
whatToDo: Follow local regulations.

name: Sablefish
idTips: Dark gray-black body, smooth skin, two dorsal fins.
whatToDo: Follow current Alaska/Pacific regulations.
